editorials.title: Beyond Bengaluru: Can Karnataka Turn Tech Power into Governance Delivery?
editorials.passage:
Speed. That evokes a thrill in all of us. But in the Indian governance context, speed needs a massive injection of the thing that powers speed: delivery.

For an investor, that can make a very real difference. Setting up a company in India can be completed within a day or two. But getting from the “I want to invest” phase to the “I am operational” phase can still mean navigating land, construction, environmental, fire, utilities and, above all, bureaucracy. It often involves different departments.

A Karnataka state-commissioned study found that some industrial projects could still take up to 450 days to get off the ground. In Dubai, the government’s Basher platform says a business can be established in as little as 15 minutes. Singapore’s online system similarly allows straightforward companies to be registered in 15 minutes.

Karnataka has been trying to change that through its single-window system and by cutting approval timelines. It is against this backdrop that the governance pitch of Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar becomes worthy of our attention.

It’s not often that an American diplomat showers praise on an Indian city and its vibrancy. When US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor recently said Bengaluru was “the perfect place to build and deliver”, he was praising something that has been decades in the making.

It is no secret that Bengaluru is a city blessed with extraordinary technological talent, a deep pool of engineers, global companies, start-ups, universities and an ecosystem that has made the city one of the world’s most important technology centres.

In fact, very few people realise that Bengaluru’s technological advantage goes back much further than the current AI boom — or even India’s current semiconductor manufacturing push. Long before India began seriously trying to build a chip-manufacturing ecosystem from 2022 onwards, Bengaluru had already become a global centre for semiconductor design, one of the most crucial parts of the chip-making process.

Texas Instruments set up its India operation in 1985, followed by companies such as Intel, Analog Devices, Synopsys and others. For decades, engineers in the city have been designing chips and semiconductor technologies for products sold around the world. But, alas, they did it largely for global US companies. Indians simply couldn’t afford them. The Karnataka government is now hoping to leverage that home-grown talent pool.

There was another part of the American ambassador’s observation that was perhaps even more interesting.

“Bengaluru doesn’t wait around, and neither does the administration.”

For Shivakumar, that is almost an endorsement of the governance model he is trying to build. It is too early to say whether it will work. Many of his biggest initiatives remain works in progress. But there is a clear idea behind them: make Karnataka faster, more technology-driven and more accessible, while using Bengaluru’s global reputation to attract the next generation of investment.

The most obvious expression of that ambition is artificial intelligence. In July, Shivakumar announced plans for India’s first government-driven AI University, along with an AI Hub intended to support research, innovation and start-ups. The state is also looking at AI infrastructure, including green data centres, and has been talking about integrating AI into governance, education and public services.

His aim is to attract companies using AI. His bigger aim is to make the technology part of Karnataka’s broader economic and administrative architecture.

It has come at a time when AI is being hotly debated across the globe for a very different reason. Researchers at Anthropic have warned that advanced AI could potentially pose an existential threat to humanity. One current Anthropic researcher, Evan Hubinger, has put the probability of AI killing all humans within the next decade at more than 10 per cent. Other researchers and technology leaders have raised concerns about increasingly autonomous systems escaping human control.

US President Donald Trump was asked about those warnings this week.

“I am not worried at all,” he said. His concern was different.

“If we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position,” Trump said, arguing that the United States currently leads China by “quite a bit”, or roughly a year.

The AI race is increasingly being viewed simultaneously as an economic opportunity, a geopolitical contest and a potential existential risk. Karnataka is undoubtedly in the first two conversations. But its challenge will be to ensure that it does not ignore the third.

The state already has an enormous head start. Bengaluru has a vast technology ecosystem, a deep engineering talent pool and thousands of start-ups and global capability centres. Karnataka has long been one of the principal engines of India’s technology economy.

In my view, the main challenge for Shivakumar is how to turn that inherited advantage into the next phase of Karnataka’s contribution to the Indian economy.

And that explains his approach: reducing the friction between government and business.

Karnataka’s investment machinery has been moving towards a more integrated single-window system, while the government has been cutting timelines for individual approvals. It says, for example, that land-use clearance has been reduced from 120 days to 45, fire NOCs from 60 to 21 days, and factory-plan and electrical approvals to 14 and 10 days respectively.

These may sound like dry administrative reforms. But they are not.

The early investment announcements suggest that companies continue to see Karnataka as a compelling destination. But what people miss is that the chief minister may be attempting to take the Karnataka story beyond Bengaluru.

Shivakumar has spoken of identifying cities outside the capital for industrial development, with the aim of creating jobs and attracting investment beyond Bengaluru. And it makes sense. Karnataka cannot forever depend on one extraordinary city to carry an entire state.

Bengaluru’s success has created its own contradictions: congestion, expensive real estate, pressure on infrastructure and an increasingly difficult urban environment. The next phase of Karnataka’s economic story therefore has to be about spreading opportunity without diluting the ecosystem that made Bengaluru successful.

There is also a more old-fashioned element to Shivakumar’s approach — and perhaps the most politically important one.

Praja Seva is an attempt to make his government more visible and accessible outside government offices. His idea is that officials should go to people rather than expecting citizens to navigate a maze of offices.

The new Praja Seva campaign, launched recently, envisages officials and elected representatives meeting people at taluk levels, hearing grievances and, where possible, resolving them on the spot or within a defined time. The government has brought grievance redressal, administrative reforms and citizen-service functions together under the new Praja Seva Department.

It’s an interesting situation.

On one side, Karnataka wants to make it easier for a multinational company to deal with the state. On the other, it says an ordinary citizen should not have to spend days moving from one government office to another.

Ease of doing business and ease of being governed are, in the end, two sides of the same coin.

This could be an emerging Shivakumar model. It is not simply pro-business. Nor is it simply about digitising the government. It is an attempt to make the state more responsive to investors at one end and citizens at the other.

But there is an important disclaimer.

None of this means Karnataka has suddenly solved governance. The state continues to face familiar problems: allegations of corruption, uneven public services and the immense infrastructure challenge posed by Bengaluru itself.

The government will ultimately be judged not by the number of policies it has announced, but by what changes those policies bring about on the ground.

The same is true of AI.

An AI university announced is not an AI university functioning. An investment commitment is not a factory employing people. A single-window portal does not automatically eliminate bureaucratic discretion. And an AI system introduced into government is not necessarily an improvement unless it makes government faster, fairer, corruption-free or more effective.

More importantly, the AI race cannot be reduced to a race for technological supremacy.

For Karnataka, the ongoing AI debate should be an opportunity rather than a constraint. A state trying to build an AI economy has a chance to build the institutions around it at the same time.

It could build stronger data governance, better AI literacy, independent oversight, responsible use of AI in public services and a workforce capable not merely of using the technology but understanding its consequences.

That would give “AI-native Karnataka” a meaning beyond attracting data centres and technology companies.

Perhaps the most important word in the emerging Karnataka narrative is not “Silicon Valley”, nor even “AI”.

It is delivery.

The world already knows that Karnataka can build technology.

The challenge for the Karnataka government now is to ensure that, in the age of AI, moving fast and moving carefully will have to happen at the same time.

<em>(The author is a Sony Award-winning journalist, with nearly 30 years at the BBC, working across London, Washington DC, and South Asia.)</em>

editorials.title: Vanishing Ground ~ I
editorials.passage:
On 17 February 2026 the National Green Tribunal refused to treat Ghoramara as permanent. Hearing a matter that had begun with a newspaper’s warning that some 40 per cent of the island could vanish by 2042, the Tribunal recorded that the Indian Sundarbans had lost, on the Geological Survey of India’s own reckoning placed before it, more than 250 square kilometres of land between 1969 and 2019 ~ Ghoramara alone falling from 8.59 to 3.83 square kilometres over those fifty years ~ and directed a joint committee to prepare, within three months, a comprehensive plan of coastal defence and resettlement. 

About four thousand people still live on what remains of the island. The tide, as ever, had not waited on the cause list. The Tribunal’s alarm is not eccentric. A peer-reviewed study in npj Climate Action, published in March 2026 by Jyotirmoy Biswas and Sabyasachi Maiti, read thirty-five years of satellite imagery from 1988 to 2023 and found the delta’s southern, sea-facing shorelines retreating faster than the rest ~ more than thirty metres a year along stretches of the eroding coast, and above fifty on the islands of Jambudwip and Bhangaduni ~ and its authors, tellingly, name managed retreat among the responses worth planning for. 

The delta is squeezed from two directions at once: its sea level is rising faster than the global average even as the low islands themselves subside, and each spring tide drives salt further into soils that once grew paddy. Ghoramara is only the sharpest case. Reuters reported in 2024 that its population had fallen from about 7,000 to some 4,000 in the single decade to 2020, the young leaving first; the neighbouring island of Lohachara slipped off usable maps in the 1990s. On Mousuni, a little to the west, households have shifted their homes inland more than once as the bank fell in behind them. Long before an island vanishes outright, the sea has usually taken the livelihood, and families begin the slow drift to the mainland fringes of Kolkata as labourers, one household at a time, in a movement no register records as displacement. 

The first thing to grasp is what these people are not. They are not, whatever the headlines call them, refugees: the word in international law means a person who has crossed a border fleeing persecution, and India is in any case not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Nor are they, in any enforceable sense, internally displaced persons, for the Republic has no statute that defines the category or attaches a single entitlement to it. The numbers that would make the omission unignorable are themselves only estimates ~ published analyses of the Indian Sundarbans have projected that as many as a million people may need to relocate from its more vulnerable islands by 2050 ~ but the absence of a firm, current count is part of the problem, not an argument against it. 

A citizen the State does not count is a citizen the State need not resettle. Nor is the gap for want of a recent look at the law. Parliament amended the Disaster Management Act in 2025 ~ the amended Act, in force from that April, broadens the vocabulary of hazard, exposure and rehabilitation and obliges the national and state authorities to take stock of emerging risks, including those from extreme climate events. Yet it still creates no status called climate migrant; its relief architecture remains built for the named catastrophe, and its very definition of evacuation is a temporary move to safety, not the permanent unmaking of a home. Two private members’ Bills of 2022 tried to supply what the amendment omitted. 

The Climate Migrants (Protection and Rehabilitation) Bill, moved by the Assam parliamentarian Pradyut Bordoloi, would have defined the internally displaced climate migrant, established a national climatemigration authority and a dedicated fund, and mandated periodic surveys in vulnerable districts; a companion Bill proposed a national committee on the displaced and a schedule of rehabilitation entitlements, from housing and land to identity documents. Both lapsed, unenacted, with the last Lok Sabha. The vocabulary already sits on the order paper. It has simply never been made law. The State is not, for all that, inert; it is merely episodic. After Cyclone Aila breached hundreds of kilometres of the delta’s embankments in 2009, West Bengal mounted relief, as it has after every major storm since. From the 1970s it resettled families from Lohachara and a shrinking Ghoramara onto Sagar Island, providing land and housing - until the land itself ran short, the entitlements thinned, and the scheme lapsed in the 1990s.

 More recently, across the state border in Odisha, the government built what has been described as India’s first climate-resettlement colony at Bagapatia, in Kendrapara, rehabilitating some 751 households from seven eroding villages of the Satabhaya region. But relief after a cyclone, and a colony raised by administrative sanction, are acts of executive grace ~ discretionary, uneven, revocable ~ and not enforceable rights. A benefit that hangs on an administrator’s goodwill is precisely what a right is not; and Bagapatia’s resettled families, moved onto poorer land with promised livelihoods that never quite materialised, are the standing proof that resettlement without entitlement is only displacement by another name. Here, then, is the gap the title names: the citizen of the vanishing delta has a popular label ~ climate refugee ~ that the law does not recognise, and a constitutional dignity that the law has not yet been made to honour. 

(The writer is a practising Chartered Accountant and a Vedantic Scholar. He can be reached at kannan@cakt.in)

editorials.title: India’s AI playbook defies Silicon Valley
editorials.passage:
Earlier this year, the corridors of Bharat Mandapam buzzed with the phrase “populationscale impact” as the India AI Impact Summit brought together civil society, government, and experts to shape AI’s trajectory for humanity. However, this is not a mere agenda item limited to panel discussions. It is showing up in real-world products and services, being developed by a rapidly evolving ecosystem. 

India is charting a new path, radically different from the prevailing global trends. In a nation home to a sixth of the world’s population, and across much of the Global South, aspiration sits uncomfortably alongside uneven access, low digital literacy, and gaps in last-mile connectivity. Big Tech services have been mostly designed for scale and not necessarily to serve the diversity of needs and constraints that are intrinsic to the Global South. Deploying AI for scale needs a very different playbook, one informed by lessons from India’s own experience. A recent analysis of nearly 110 home-grown startups and non-profits building AI for impact at scale reveals a decentralised landscape. It is shaped by solutions built around communityspecific problems, rather than chasing scale for its own sake. 

In contrast to the ‘bigger is better’ ethos of Silicon Valley, a new generation of founders is building full-stack AI start-ups tailored to domestic realities. A distinct playbook for populationscale impact in India is emerging, defined by three conditions: localisation, offline-compatible design, and voicefirst AI. The first condition is localisation. In India, impact often means reaching rural populations, where barriers are not just technical, but economic, linguistic, and infrastructural. Solutions must be designed for low-connectivity environments, intuitive interactions, and affordability. Moreover, the hinterland is not a monolith and cannot be treated as a single market. It is a complex ecosystem requiring deeply contextual design developed in tandem with communities. Consider agriculture. 

Local farms represent one of the world’s largest opportunities for decision intelligence, where integrating weather data, soil insights, and market signals can enable more resilient and efficient food systems. Platforms like DeHaat are doing exactly this, combining AI-driven agronomy models with satellite data and soil analytics to deliver personalised, multilingual recommendations to smallholder farmers. Delivered through a simple mobile interface, such solutions demonstrate what localised, last-mile AI can look like at scale - already supporting over a million farmers across multiple states. The second condition is building offline, on-device AI. 

In India, mass adoption depends on solutions that can function with or without always-on connectivity, processing data locally, as opposed to relying on the cloud. For most users, this distinction is invisible, yet it determines whether a product works at all. This shift is pushing start-ups to think beyond lightweight ‘wrappers on existing AI models’ towards full-stack solutions that combine AI with hardware, IoT, and offline connectivity. When AI operates offline and directly on a device, it offers two key benefits: it makes systems viable in lowconnectivity settings to reduce inference costs, and offers control over privacy and security. Netradyne applies this by moving processing from the cloud into the vehicle; its fleet safety system uses on-device AI to monitor driving time and identify risk signals like fatigue or lane deviation, triggering real-time audio alerts for self-correction. Similarly, Pinky Promise, a healthtech platform designed for women, offers 24/7 AI-driven guidance on reproductive health. 

Created for low-bandwidth environments, it enables women in rural areas to access medical advice without the need to travel far, incur high costs, or navigate social stigma. Solutions like Pinky Promise, which serves over 150,000 Indian women, were built to work offline and demonstrate how AI can expand access to essential services where traditional tools fall short. The third condition is voice-first AI. Multilingual AI solutions are unlocking innovation in niche sectors like JusticeTech. The national justice system is constrained by long wait times, legal complexity, limited availability of information in local languages, and knowledge asymmetry. 

Millions of citizens stand to benefit from understanding legal notices, welfare entitlements, and government communications. Jugalbandi, a free multilingual AI assistant, helps people understand and access government schemes, public services, and legal recourse through voice-first interaction in their native languages, making critical information more accessible. Voice AI is perhaps the most intuitive interface, enabling people to use built-for-purpose AI solutions in a way that feels accessible, convenient, and light-touch. Several organisations in the country, such as Bhashini and Sarvam, are building multilingual language models for specific use cases, and as shared capabilities that can work across platforms, scale across contexts, and be reused across applications. Together, these three conditions point to a distinct model, shaped by how people actually live, work, and access technology. 

The start-up ecosystem is innovating solutions that are purpose-built, locally embedded, and designed for specific use cases. Their strength lies in their ability to work reliably across diverse and often underserved environments. This gives them the superpower to scale meaningfully across a diversity of contexts. As the ecosystem evolves, questions around long-term sustainability, feasibility, and impact potential will remain critical. Not all solutions will endure, and not all experiments will translate into lasting impact. 

Yet, the direction is clear: a growing number of start-ups and organisations are building with a deep understanding of the environments they operate in, and are designing accordingly. India’s approach offers a useful playbook for the Global South, contexts where access and infrastructure remain uneven. The future of AI will be shaped as much by how systems are built and deployed as by the technology itself. 

(The writers are, respectively, Founder and CEO, and Consultant at Kalpa Impact and co-authors of India’s AI Impact Startups)

editorials.title: Algorithms make the spade infra dig
editorials.passage:
Gone are the days when archaeologists used classical tools and technology to reveal the history buried in relics, including manuscripts. The history of archaeology is inseparable from the evolution of technology. Each generation of tools has expanded our ability to uncover ancient structures, relics, and manuscripts, transforming archaeology from a discipline of manual excavation into one of digital revelation, which occasionally rewrites history. 

In the classical era, discovery was a matter of physical endurance. Archaeologists relied on picks, shovels, and brushes to expose ruins, while epigraphists (specialists who study and decipher inscriptions engraved on durable materials such as stone, metal, pottery, or shell) copied inscriptions by hand. These methods, though pioneering, were slow, invasive, and often destructive. Fragile manuscripts and artefacts were easily damaged, and much knowledge was lost in the process. The scientific revolution of the 19th and 20th centuries introduced precision and preservation. 

Photography and films provided faithful documentation of sites; radiocarbon dating established reliable timelines. Modern approaches emphasise non-destructive or minimally invasive techniques such as X-ray fluorescence (XRF), Raman spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR), and mass spectrometry, which reveal composition, corrosion, pigments, and binders without damaging the artefact. Remote sensing began to map landscapes from above. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) allowed scholars to visualise settlement patterns, while 3D scanning and photogrammetry (the technology of extracting reliable 3D measurements and models from overlapping 2D photographs) created digital replicas of monuments and artefacts. Archaeology is becoming less destructive, more analytical, and increasingly interdisciplinary as technology advances. 

Today, in the AI era, discovery has entered a new dimension. Machine learning algorithms sift through satellite imagery to detect anomalies that may conceal buried structures. Predictive models forecast excavation hotspots, guiding archaeologists to promising sites with remarkable efficiency. AI-assisted restoration revives eroded inscriptions and manuscripts, reconstructing missing words by learning from linguistic and stylistic patterns. Neural networks classify pottery and tools by cultural origin, accelerating research that once took decades to accomplish. Meanwhile, virtual and augmented reality recreate ancient cities and manuscripts, allowing immersive exploration by scholars and the public alike. 

India boasts of the largest known collection of ancient and medieval manuscripts. But many remain unread due to the painstaking manual labour needed to decipher them. The Asiatic Society in Kolkata, established in 1874, which is a treasure house of old manuscripts, contains more than 52,000 manuscripts, many of which have remained undeciphered so far. They have recently started transliteration of the manuscripts using machine learning to make these texts accessible to scholars worldwide, ensuring their survival for future generations. To train and validate these models, researchers utilise handwritten manuscripts that are available in digitised form; some of which date back to many centuries BC. A startling recent revelation is that a 12th century sculpture at Dhar in Madhya Pradesh, known as the goddess Saraswati, has now been identified as the goddess Gayatri, who personifies the Gayatri Mantra and Vedic wisdom. 

The sculpture was unearthed in the late 19th century, with one of the upper hands damaged. Scholars assumed that it held a veena, Saraswati’s defining attribute. Both Saraswati and Gayatri share the same vahana (swan), which reinforced the idea of Saraswati. Also, both of them are linked to wisdom, learning, and Vedic knowledge. The revelation transpired through the use of precise digital documentation and high-resolution 3D mapping of the red sandstone sculpture, which identified the Vedas and not a book, a lotus and not a rosary, and decoded iconographic clues that had remained unnoticed for centuries. The trajectory from ‘spade to algorithm’ underscores a profound truth: technology does not replace human insight but amplifies it. Archaeologists, along with historians, remain the interpreters of context, culture, and meaning. And with digital tools and artificial intelligence, the past is no longer confined to fragile ruins or fading manuscripts. It is now preserved, illuminated, and made accessible to the whole world, ensuring that ancient voices continue to resonate in the modern age. History is being rewritten by technology. 

(The writer is an author and columnist.)

editorials.title: Pacing the race
editorials.passage:
The most consequential warning about artificial intelligence may now be coming from the people most invested in building it. Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, has argued that frontier AI development needs to proceed slower, with stronger independent scrutiny. The significance lies less in the proposal itself than in what it reveals: the technology race is beginning to collide with the limits of human institutions. This is not an argument for abandoning AI. 

Nor is it a plea for technological nostalgia. AI could transform medicine, scientific research, education and productivity. But the assumption that every increase in capability is automatically desirable is becoming harder to defend. When systems acquire unexpected abilities, including the capacity to exploit vulnerabilities or operate with increasing autonomy, the consequences of a mistake can extend beyond the laboratory. The problem is that commercial competition rewards speed. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and other frontier developers have enormous financial incentives to release more capable systems before rivals do. Governments, meanwhile, have their own strategic incentives. 

The United States sees advanced AI as an instrument of economic and military power; China regards technological self-reliance as central to its geopolitical ambitions. Neither Washington nor Beijing is naturally inclined to slow down if it believes the other side will continue accelerating. That creates a dangerous paradox. The greater the perceived strategic importance of AI, the harder restraint becomes. A company that voluntarily slows its development could simply lose ground to a competitor. 

A country that restrains itself unilaterally could fear surrendering technological advantage to a rival. Yet allowing that logic to dictate the pace of AI development would amount to outsourcing a political decision to market competition and geopolitical anxiety. The speed at which humanity approaches potentially transformative technology should not be determined solely by quarterly incentives or national rivalry. There is also a legitimate danger in allowing leading AI companies to define the rules themselves. Safety standards designed by incumbents can unintentionally become barriers protecting incumbents. Regulation must therefore be independent, transparent and applicable across the industry, including powerful established companies and open-source developers. 

The answer is not an indefinite moratorium. It is institutional capacity proportional to technological power. Frontier models should face genuinely independent testing, meaningful disclosure of serious safety incidents and common standards for assessing dangerous capabilities. Governments should coordinate internationally rather than treating AI safety exclusively as a contest between national champions. The history of nuclear technology offers an uncomfortable precedent. Once a technology became capable of threatening civilisation itself, national competition could not simply be wished away; it had to be contained. 

AI may not follow the nuclear path. But the lesson is relevant: when technological capability begins to outrun the institutions capable of governing it, speed ceases to be an uncomplicated virtue. The test for the AI industry is therefore not whether it can build machines more powerful than before. It is whether humanity can build safeguards quickly enough to remain in control of what those machines become.

editorials.title: The Harder Test
editorials.passage:
The Cockroach Janta Party has already achieved what few new political movements manage: it forced a powerful government to concede. The harder test is what comes next. The developments this month suggest that CJP is no longer simply a protest over examination failures. The September 5 Delhi march was called off after the Centre approached the Supreme Court and reiterated commitments concerning cases against protesters. The Court’s intervention has since acquired its own significance, with the suspension of a Greater Noida magistrate after a student received a preventive-action notice despite the Court's earlier orders. 

CJP has also pressed for the arrest of social media influencer Swatantra Bharadwaj over allegations arising from the Jantar Mantar protests. Bharadwaj is now in custody. Here again, the movement is testing whether the law will be applied consistently rather than merely demanding another political concession. That is a significant evolution. The original CJP victory came from converting anger over examination failures into political pressure. Its emerging campaign is different: it seeks to make citizens scrutinise how the state functions after the headlines have moved on.The “School Thik Karo” campaign may therefore be more consequential than another street mobilisation. 

By entering schools, documenting deficiencies and asking why basic promises remain unmet, CJP is attempting to move accountability from the exceptional moment of protest into the routine functioning of government. That is harder to dramatise, but potentially more transformative. A movement that can make scrutiny habitual could outlast the anger that created it. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke captures this change. He says the movement wants to move beyond elections and political parties towards a culture in which citizens understand their rights and duties and hold governments accountable regardless of who is in power. Its campaign to inspect rural government schools is an early attempt to turn that proposition into practice. But accountability cannot be one-directional. 

CJP has already experienced an internal split, with a breakaway faction accusing its leadership of politicisation and centralisation. It has also faced a legal challenge after posts containing a false attribution were circulated. These episodes may be uncomfortable, but they are also useful tests. A movement demanding accountability from institutions must eventually demonstrate that it can subject itself to the same standards. The same principle applies to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s revival of the “Dimagi Naxal” label at the Shri Ram College of Commerce. CJP's response ~ that a questioning generation needs hope rather than labels ~ captures the movement's larger challenge to political language. 

The government can dismiss a protest. It is harder to dismiss a generation that has learned to ask questions. But the CJP too must learn that questioning power is easier than exercising power responsibly. Its future will depend not on how loudly it protests, but on whether it can build a credible, evidence-based and politically independent culture of accountability. The July victory made CJP famous. What it does with that victory will determine whether it becomes consequential.

editorials.title: Slow poison
editorials.passage:
Arguing before a court in New Mexico earlier this year, Meta’s lawyers used the image of a polluting factory. If a factory fouls the air, they submitted, the proper remedy is to make it cease its emissions and to clean up what it has already spoilt. It is neither to demolish the plant, nor to burden its owner with every ailment in the town downwind. It was a lawyerly attempt to limit the damage in the event Meta lost to the state of New Mexico in a case where the state claimed that its platforms, specifically Instagram, were responsible for the mental health crisis amongst youth.

In his ruling last month, Judge Bryan Biedscheid took the image and turned it elegantly against its author. Meta’s platforms were the factory, the content they served was what the factory produced, and the psychological harm to, and sexual exploitation of, children was the pollution that had to be abated. On that reasoning he did something no court anywhere had done before — he declared certain activities of the social media company to have caused a public nuisance.

Dwell on the judge’s picture a little and the smoke from the factory acquires a name. Two names, in particular: the infinite scroll and the push notification. Neither is an accident of engineering; both are its object. The infinite scroll exists, amongst other things, to keep a child’s thumb moving. The push notification seeks to reignite a child’s attention long after the child has wished to stop. The disease that settles in the lungs is by now familiar and backed up by evidence — anxiety, sleeplessness, depression, self-harm. This is the first thing to be said plainly, and Judge Biedscheid said it: the harm is not incidental to the design, it is the design itself. Addiction is the product; the anxiety is its exhaust.

Days after the ruling, Meta reached for its chequebook. To end other litigations on youth mental health claims, it agreed to pay a staggering $18.2 billion to 52 American states and territories in the largest technology settlement in American history. However, on reading the document, a familiar sleight of hand appears. Meta admits nothing — not a single whiff of wrongdoing. That is at once the genius and the vice of the settlement: one pays, precisely, to make the question disappear. American law permits a company to purchase silence and keep its conscience unexamined, and then calls that transaction justice. This isn’t justice, it is a cash memo.

Were a factory’s effluents to poison a town’s water supply, would we let it write a cheque to pay the municipal council, at the same time not admit it had poisoned anyone, and keep its pipes running? Yet, where the contaminated thing is a child’s mind, this is exactly the absurd bargain the settlement endorses — pay, deny, continue. The wrong is not undone, it is merely priced.

The price too is at a heavy discount. Sample this — of the $18.2 billion, only some 70%, around $12.7 billion, is committed; the balance is contingent and turns on Meta’s rivals falling into line. Spread that committed sum across the 10 years it is owed and it comes to roughly $1.3 billion a year, levied on a company that clocked $201 billion in revenue and $60 billion in profit last year alone. It is less than 1% of a single year’s takings. Meta will possibly spend more on data centres this coming year than it will ever pay these children. No wonder its share price in the stock market surged after the settlement, investors presumably relieved by the relatively small size of the payout.

Worse, the settlement leaves the engine largely untouched. Admittedly, some adjustments have been ordered in relation to teen users — night curfews, daily time limits, and an “option” to switch to a non-personalised feed. But the basic feature of infinite scrolling and notifications continues undisturbed. The factory continues operating, the content continues to be produced, just that the shifts get a little shorter.

What this means for India begins with a platitude — the mental health of an Indian child is worth no less than that of an American one. The arithmetic follows readily enough. The American payout approximates to $250 per child. India has some 430 million children and valued at the same rate, for the same injury, at the hands of the same company, the figure exceeds $100 billion — half a year of Meta’s global revenue, a sum large enough to be felt in Menlo Park.

It is time for a well-crafted litigation to hold Meta and similar companies liable for public nuisance in Indian courts. Our law of tort is no stranger to public nuisance; our children are no strangers to the injury; and the factory, it bears repeating, is the very same factory that exists in the United States of America. To be clear — this is not about Meta. The principle indicts every so-called platform that sends engineered content to the young by design, harming them often irredeemably.

While contemplating legal action, it is equally important to reflect on how we arrived at this pass. It all started with a simple error of nomenclature. Long ago we agreed to call these enterprises ‘platforms’ — neutral, passive noticeboards upon which others pinned their notices. Having so named them, we clothed them in immunity for what others post on it. In America it was Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act; in India, it is the safe harbour of Section 79 of the Information Technology Act. The intermediary, we solemnly held, was a conduit, and not a publisher, the post office and not the printer. That was the original sin. Today, Instagram no more hosts content than a chef at a restaurant hosts a meal. It prepares, it chooses, and it decides what is served to you.

Consider, by contrast, a factory that makes cakes and jams. We hold it answerable for its product — for the recipe, and for the provenance of its sugar. We do not entertain the plea that the ingredients assembled themselves. Why should a firm that manufactures a child’s attention be held to a gentler standard than one that manufactures marmalade? Get the noun right and the law follows: Instagram is not a platform but a product, and it should be regulated as one.

The lesson, moreover, is not confined to either Instagram specifically or social media generally. We are now in the throes of precisely the same argument over Artificial Intelligence — what to call it, and who shall answer when it does harm. Nomenclature is not branding; it is destiny. Misname the thing today and a generation will pay to clear the smoke.

A New Mexico judge has today seen the factory for what it is. Other states in America, on the other hand, chose to fine it and avert their gaze. India has never lacked laws to tackle pollution, just the will to enforce them effectively. One hopes that when it comes to content that pollutes the mind of children, India will have both the will and the capacity to place the interests of an innocent Indian child over those of a rapacious foreign algorithm.

Arghya Sengupta is Research Director, Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy. Views are personal

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Why do people think money can buy blessings?
editorials.passage:
Sir — Money, the adage goes, cannot buy happiness. Why then do people think that it can buy blessings? People seem to be under the impression that making expensive offerings will get divine benevolence. Take, for instance, a sweet shop in Nashik that is selling golden modaks covered in 24-carat, edible gold. They cost Rs 27,000 per kilogramme. Such ostentatiousness goes against the mythological accounts that narrate how gods are pleased with the humblest of offerings. For instance, Kubera, the god of wealth, tried to impress Ganesha with a lavish banquet. But the latter’s bottomless hunger was only satisfied when Kubera surrendered his ego and offered a simple handful of roasted rice with true humility.

Sir — I am disappointed by Amit Roy’s article on Ketaki Kushari Dyson (“A life dedicated to Tagore and literature”, Sept 14). He quotes Neil Astley that her first book of English poems appeared in Oxford in 1979. On the contrary, like many Indian poets in English, she entrusted Writers Workshop, Calcutta, with her debut collection, Sap-Wood , which we published in 1978. Even Wikipedia gets this right; a simple online fact-check or consulting her own website would have saved Roy from making this error.

We also brought out two volumes of her English translations of Kabirul Islam’s Bengali poetry — Poems (1979) and The Home-Coming (1982).

Sir — Three bilateral meetings undertaken by India during the recent BRICS Summit reflect New Delhi’s ambition to lead the Global South in economic governance and diversify partnerships to reduce reliance on any single power bloc while achieving concrete trade, currency, food and energy outcomes (“Options open”, Sept 14). In a fractured world, India’s ability to engage Tehran, Beijing and Moscow while keeping ties with Washington and Europe alive is a rare diplomatic asset.

Sir — Despite sharing a long border, India and China have a complicated relationship marked by territorial disputes over Arunachal Pradesh and strategic tensions regarding Pakistan. However, both economic giants recognise that long-term hostility hinders growth. This has prompted efforts to discuss bilateral issues and stabilise relations. As core members of BRICS alongside nations like Russia and South Africa, they share a powerful platform that accounts for a substantial portion of global trade, allowing them to cooperate on international commercial challenges.

Sir — The New Delhi Declaration at the 18th BRICS Summit is a significant diplomatic victory for India, forging common ground on restraint, civilian protection and sovereignty despite sharp differences among members over West Asia (“Rare bridge”, Sept 15). This consensus underscores the continuing relevance of BRICS as a voice of the Global South. But declarations alone cannot reshape the global order. The real test is whether commitments to make governance more representative translate into concrete investments and measurable outcomes.

M. Jeyaram, Sholavandan, Tamil Nadu

Sir — It is worth noting that several of the historians discussed in the article, “History lessons” (Sept 14), wrote substantially in Bengali. They thus deserve greater recognition when it comes to our understanding of the intellectual history of Bengal. Perhaps Jayanta Sengupta should have also remembered historians who devoted virtually their entire professional lives to the discipline and taught in Calcutta, but whose names are increasingly being forgotten. I can think of Amales Tripathi, Chittabrata Palit, Sushil Chaudhury, Sunil Sen, Amalendu De and the recently deceased Ranjit Sen.

Intellectual history cannot be reconstructed only through the names that subsequently became nationally or internationally famous. There were scholars who spent decades teaching, researching, supervising students, working in archives and writing serious history but who did not acquire the same visibility within metropolitan academic networks. Their contribution to historical scholarship in Bengal is still substantial.

Sir — In his article, Jayanta Sengupta pays tribute to five historians: Ranajit Guha, Tapan Raychaudhuri, Ashin Das Gupta, Sabyasachi Bhattacharya and Sumit Sarkar. The article reminds us that real history takes a lifetime of patience and constant critical doubt regarding all certainties. The article could have given a few present-day examples that would have stoked doubts about certainties that people seem to have gained from WhatsApp University these days.

Sukhendu Bhattacharjee, Hooghly

Sir — Countries that have contributed most to global greenhouse-gas emissions cannot escape responsibility for the growing climate crisis. While climate change affects the entire world, its consequences are deeply unequal. Poor and developing countries, which have contributed relatively little to emissions historically, are often the victims of natural calamities. Nepal’s ongoing suffering is case in point.

Gregory Fernandes, Mumbai

Sir — Kathmandu is right to demand $20 million in immediate climate compensation and broader reparations from major greenhouse gas emitters like China, India, and the United States of America following the devastating, late-August 2026 flash floods and mudslides. The Loss and Damage Fund set up at COP27 in Sharm El-Sheikh can be dipped into for this.

editorials.title: Thirsty data centres
editorials.passage:
Artificial Intelligence is presented in an abstract manner. Algorithms learn. Models think. Cloud data flow. However, every chatbot, image generator, and predictive model has a physical infrastructure of servers, data centres, transmission networks and cooling systems behind it.

These facilities use land, electricity and/or water, depending on their cooling system. The geography of AI infrastructure could be as critical as the technology itself. An increase in data centre capacity has been observed, from approximately 375 MW in 2020 to approximately 1,500 MW by 2025.

As part of the nation’s AI compute framework, over 38,000 GPUs have been on-boarded. The government projects the electricity consumption for data centres is likely to grow to 13.56 GW by 2031-32. These statistics showcase India’s digital aspirations. But what about this infrastructure’s environmental imprint?

Over 50% of India’s data centres are in water-stressed areas as per the World Resource Institute, India; 75% of the facilities are in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.

A hint of the conflict is already apparent in Thane. There is concern of shortage of water supply for a hyper-scale data centre project at an estimated shortfall of around 30 million litres a day. According to the municipal commissioner, 12 MLD of recycled sewage water will be provided to the project. Amazon refuted allegations it would be using the water for cooling.

This conflict is more pronounced in Tusiana village of Greater Noida. A data centre park is emerging near the village whose residents have voiced concerns about the groundwater. According to Down To Earth , they were worried about threats to aquifers when the data centre complex expanded. The company, Yotta Data Services, did not use ground water or drinking water but, instead, used treated non-potable water and its cooling system was closed-loop and air-cooled.

Bengaluru has already learnt how easily water scarcity can become an everyday, urban crisis. Karnataka is also one of the five states which account for three-quarters of data centres in India.

An incident of contamination in a data centre’s fill-and-flush wastewater was linked to a rare bacteria in the reclaimed-water system in Cheyenne, Wyoming, by local wastewater officials. There was no impact on drinking water. An independent test ordered by the project’s general contractor reportedly showed no evidence of the bacterium. Cheyenne officials, however, prohibited such discharges into the city’s sewer system.

India should think about establishing a framework for disclosure of all the basic information about water sources, annual and peak usage, recycled water usage, electricity usage, cooling technology and so on for large data centres. The disclosure should be at the facility level and not limited to national sustainability reports.

Approvals may include a ‘computational carrying capacity assessment’. The same must be done for groups of digital infrastructure. Planners should consider the total water and electricity usage of existing and planned data centres prior to approving new, large data centres in areas under stress.

Incentives should be offered for both location and efficiency. Data centres are a fiercely competitive market among states. However, an advanced cooling facility in a water-constrained area could pose a higher risk over the long-term than a facility placed in a water resilient area.

A ‘resource sensitivity map for digital infrastructure’, with suggestions on how water-stressed, grid-capable and climate-resilient areas are best suited to host data centres, may also be considered.

The next digital divide is ecological. The next phase of AI policy in India should thus pose a query on top of the questions of the number of GPUs the country has, or how much data centre space it can create. It must reflect on the environmental impacts of data centres.

Anuradha P.S. is professor, department of commerce, CHRIST (deemed to be university)

editorials.title: Poll toffee: Editorial on 'revdis' crossing borders and reshaping politics
editorials.passage:
Has the revdi , synonymous with India’s poll sweeteners, travelled West? Last week, Donald Trump, the president of the United States of America, announced that every American would receive a poll dividend of 5,000 dollars only if the Republicans succeeded in holding on to both chambers of the Congress in the mid-term polls in November. The source of the funds remains unclear: the payout, if Mr Trump chooses to honour it — an earlier promise of cheques worth $2,000 to be funded by tariff revenues did not materialise — would cost the government an estimated $1.3 trillion. Will the American taxpayer shoulder the burden? The dole has undoubtedly been dangled with the imminent mid-term polls in mind that are expected to test his party sternly. Mr Trump’s decision to embroil the US in a long and costly conflict with Iran has led to rising prices in his country. But would the carrot bring about the electoral dividend that Mr Trump hopes? After all, the average annual per capita income in the US is $94,430. But a healthy per capita income does not necessarily guarantee equitable income distribution. In fact, the US Census Bureau’s American Community Survey of 2024 found that the mean annual household income for the bottom 20% of the American population amounted to $17,132. This needy constituency could be in Mr Trump’s radar.

Two interesting inferences can be drawn from these developments. First, right-wing governments around the world are no longer averse to learning from their peers — even from those in the Global South. It must be pointed out that Mr Trump has also advocated for tighter voting laws in the US in acknowledgement of India’s electoral system which, ironically, stands accused of being exclusionary in light of the developments relating to the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. This flexibility lends these regimes a degree of suppleness in terms of self-preservation. Second, and more important, is the emergence of doles — initially conceived as a welfare measure — as a potent electoral weapon cutting across ideological and political affiliations. In India, the Sixteenth Finance Commission report data suggest that mass cash transfers amounted to Rs 1.96 lakh crore in 2025-26. This blurring of lines between welfare and populism may yield electoral benefits. But a discourse on revdis cannot ignore the economic and ethical collateral damage.

editorials.title: Be Open: Editorial on AI safety and why companies cannot be their own watchdog
editorials.passage:
The chief executive officer of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, has called for a slowdown in the development of increasingly capable Artificial Intelligence systems. He has asked for government controls, including the United States of America and other democratic nations getting countries like China to accept similar limits, and coordination among tech companies to ensure that AI does not get to the stage where it outruns humans’ ability to understand or control it. The heads of OpenAI, Google DeepMind and xAI have endorsed his appeal. This comes after reports of AI agents going rogue and warnings from researchers within Anthropic about the prospect of losing control over more advanced models. These concerns are valid. Yet the proposed response is conspicuously conditional: the companies want their rivals and governments to slow down alongside them. Each could independently halt its most ambitious research but doing so would risk surrendering a commercial advantage, which clearly trumps worries about safety. China, unsurprisingly, sees the proposal, particularly the call for tighter chip export controls, as an attempt to restrict Chinese progress. The US president has rejected a slowdown so that America retains its lead over China. Warnings about danger also, ironically, increase valuations in the market eventually. OpenAI has used the warning as an excuse to postpone going public on the stock market.

Yet, none of these suspicions proves that the risks outlined by Mr Amodei are imaginary. There is indeed a strong case for reducing the pace of AI development. The pursuit of ever larger and more competent AI models consumes capital and resources. Data centres, for instance, demand considerable energy, water and physical infrastructure. These costs affect existential challenges such as global warming — 0.5% to 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions come from data centres. Questions of safety in the everyday uses of AI in defence, medicine and hospitals, law enforcement and education remain as urgent as the threat of a dystopian future. A slowdown agreed upon among a few dominant firms would leave the central problem unresolved: the public cannot assess risks that companies alone define, investigate and disclose. Independent evaluators need access that cannot be withdrawn when their findings become inconvenient. The question is whether tech companies remain amenable to facilitate greater transparency and accountability: that may harness AI to a democratic ethic.

editorials.title: Prediction markets must be reined in
editorials.passage:
We live amidst a gamification of the world. From electoral outcomes to sporting victories and celebrity breakups, every “Yes” and “No” is now an ‘event outcome’ capable of monetisation on online ‘prediction markets’ like Kalshi and Polymarket. Public discourse has, thus far, quite rightly viewed such platforms as glorified online casinos. However, recent commentary by market insiders argues that such markets serve a greater economic role as ‘information aggregators’ and ‘universal insurance’. Such arguments push for laissez faire regulation of prediction markets, and advocate their expansion and further institutionalisation. As these opinions gain traction, a comprehensive and categorical rebuttal is necessary in the interests of informed public discourse.

Proponents of prediction markets argue as follows. Prediction markets, like regular forecasting/punditry, allow people to express their informed opinions on current events. People don’t just make predictions, but are compelled to ‘put their money where their mouth is’, ensuring more informed and careful predictions. By financialising public opinion, these markets aggregate information more efficiently than regular forecasting models ever could. This creates a ‘truth machine’ that gives us a window into the future, they say.

Further, proponents also argue that these binary Yes/No bets (called ‘event contracts’) offer a revolutionary new way to hedge against real-world risk. If you can bet against an election result that might impact your life negatively, you are ‘insuring’ yourself against the consequences, they say.

This comparison with insurance is where the case for laissez faire prediction markets begins to fall apart. Legally speaking, the difference between an insurance contract and a speculative wager is the existence of insurable interest in the underlying event. Simply put, a contract that pays me if my house burns down is an insurance contract because I have a vested interest in ensuring my house doesn’t burn down. Absent this vested interest, a contract that, let’s say, pays me if a stranger’s house burns down, is a purely speculative wager, better known as… a gamble. The doctrine of insurable interest has an expansive and sophisticated ambit, encompassing a wide range of personal and commercial risks. Therefore, where genuine risks exist, regulated insurance markets are usually fully equipped to help mitigate them. Prediction markets do away with this crucial doctrine entirely, allowing people to monetise outcomes they aren’t directly impacted by. Legally speaking, this is gambling, plain and simple. It is a fundamental economic principle (Posner, et al .) that mandating insurable interest in contingent contracts ensures that such contracts only hedge against existing risk, and don’t create new risk. The reason is fairly intuitive.

Most tradeable investment contracts (shares, bonds, etc.) are what economists call positive-sum transactions. For instance, when an investor buys a company’s bonds, the money so raised is used by the company to do business, make a profit, and return some part thereof to the investor as interest. This is a ‘win-win’ situation that creates wealth and facilitates economic growth. Event contracts on the other hand, are zero-sum games, i.e., what one party wins, the other necessarily loses. There is no economic activity underlying these bets, which create no wealth and facilitate no growth. In light of this vital difference, the strongest case against legalising/institutionalising prediction markets is not a moral diatribe against gambling, but basic economics.

In a bid to overcome this objection, proponents point to derivative markets (futures, options, swaps, etc.). They argue that speculators are routinely allowed to trade zero-sum oil futures or forex swaps without trading the underlying oil or foreign exchange, so why this double standard? This is a tempting, yet fallacious argument.

Derivative markets for securities/commodities exist precisely because transactions in the underlying securities/commodities are positive-sum. Speculation on derivative markets is grudgingly tolerated as a necessary evil so that genuine businesspeople can find counterparties to their hedges easily and at a variety of price points. Prediction markets on the other hand, support no positive-sum economic activity whatsoever, and the question of tolerating speculation as a necessary evil simply does not arise.

This is a small price to pay for the ‘truth machine’, proponents persist. Telling the future surely cannot be of zero economic value! But far from telling the future, prediction markets create deeply perverse incentives that reward active sabotage in the real world. When the payout for an event occurring exceeds the cost of making that event occur, each bet mobilizes an army of bounty hunters looking to ‘fix’ outcomes. The dangers of such manipulation in the real world are grave, extend well beyond the economy, and are already starting to be seen.

The tradability of event contracts on exchanges also raises concerns of insider trading, where people with non-public information about events unfairly use such information to profit at the market’s expense. A market compromised by widespread manipulation and insider trading cannot yield a reliable truth signal.

Proponents brush these concerns aside, arguing that prediction markets will be tightly regulated just like existing securities markets. This naively ignores the impossibly large scale of the regulatory state required to make such markets fair and transparent. A regulator would have to monitor every world event, every stakeholder involved in said event, prevent sabotage, and ensure that ‘insiders’ (once somehow identified) are not trading on non-public information. This is practically impossible, and moreover, for a zero-sum activity, a colossal waste of state capacity. Investigating and punishing manipulation and insider trading in securities markets is already a highly complicated and technical endeavour, requiring significant public investment. Modern regulations mandate continuous insider disclosures, information-flow tracking, and algorithmic trade monitoring. Regulation along these lines for prediction markets is inconceivable at scale, and would render privacy rights meaningless.

The widespread growth and institutionalisation of prediction markets will bring about an unprecedented drain on productive capital. It will turn the real world into a gamified nightmare, with every bet subject to widespread sabotage and bounty hunting. In a world where fair and effective regulation is impossible, we must ensure these markets do not gain a strong legal foothold in any growth-oriented economy, regardless of nationality, jurisdiction or regulatory environment. Growth is built, not wagered.

The writer is a corporate and tax lawyer based in Chennai

Published on September 16, 2026

editorials.title: Decoding BRICS’ energy intent
editorials.passage:
We acknowledge fossil fuels will still play an important role in the world’s energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies, and we recognize the need to promote just, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitions and reduce GHG emissions in line with our climate goals and observing SDG7, and the principles of technological neutrality and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities taking into account national circumstances, needs and priorities,” reads BRICS New Delhi Declaration of September 12, 2026.

By validating the ongoing importance of fossil fuels, the declaration provides the energy sector with a critical defence: it rejects an aggressive phase-out in favour of a realistic, managed transition, which, some say, is good for India, Russia and Saudi Arabia.

But this should not be seen as a free pass to energy-import reliant nations like India. What BRICS membership actually does is provide vital diplomatic leverage: it keeps India and Iran at the negotiating table, safeguarding India’s access to the strategic Chabahar Port.

Energy security: Ensuring energy market stability and maintaining undisrupted flows of energy from diverse sources, strengthening value chains. This is a priority after West Asia conflict.

Digital and Smart Grids: BRICS pushed AI, data analytics for grid management.

Diversified mix: Declaration lists all sources as important — renewable energy, bioenergy, fossil fuels, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, low carbon technologies, energy storage.

Critical Minerals Focus on reliable supply chains for lithium, cobalt, copper, but with sovereign rights of resource countries.

Local currencies: Finally, Energy Ministers called for use of local currencies in energy trade.

The declaration provides for Smart Grids & Storage Centre in India; Push for Global Biofuels Alliance; reliable and stable supply chains for minerals. India needs lithium for EVs, solar, semiconductors.

In the wake of ongoing West Asia conflicts and Red Sea disruptions, India wants to insulate its economy by sourcing crude oil from Russia, the Gulf, or the US without the threat of unilateral sanctions. The BRICS Energy Ministers’ parallel push for local currency trade offers a vital financial shield.

Settling transactions in rupees, rubles, or dirhams reduces US dollar dependency, minimises exposure to secondary sanctions, and structurally protects India’s foreign exchange reserves. RBI already has rupee settlement mechanism for Russian oil.

With the West Asia conflict disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, the declaration’s emphasis on “diverse sources” provides India with the diplomatic leverage to source oil from Russia, the US, the UAE, and Iraq. Whether this strategic framing explains why New Delhi persistently purchased discounted Russian crude despite heavy Western pressure remains a question only the Ministry of External Affairs can answer.

Protection of critical energy infrastructure, including cross-border infrastructure is a boostfor India as this means undersea cables, LNG terminals, proposed India-Middle East-Europe pipeline, and power grid connections with Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh could be in offing.

The declaration can even be seen as an endorsement of India’s approach: keep coal and gas for baseload, add solar and wind rapidly, secure oil from cheapest source, and build storage.

However, there are challenges. BRICS is opposed to EU’s carbon tax, but EU’s CBAM has kicked in from January 1, 2026. Indian steel and aluminium will still pay at EU border from this year. India will need to take this up at WTO and build its own carbon credit system fast. Clearly, just a joint statement won’t stop the tax. India ramped up Russian oil purchases — from 2 per cent to 35 per cent — because it was cheap ($20-30 discount), but that is now down to $3-5 a barrel.

India will get hurt if it gets too reliant on one supplier and US tightens secondary sanctions. Energy security implies diversification of supply sources, not substituting West Asian dependence with Russian dependence.

The Declaration talks about resilient supply chains, but India has no lithium, cobalt, nickel processing. India’s Critical Mineral Mission needs to secure mines in Brazil, South Africa, Argentina, not just MOUs.

A critical question is, will Iran allow free and smooth access? On the face of it Iran is not blocking, but inviting transit right now. The greater risk is not Iran but US sanctions.

Hormuz right now is technically open but practically almost closed. Iran wants to resume oil sales to India to broaden its buyer pool beyond China and India is pushing Chabahar as an alternative to Hormuz, open to Arabian Sea.

Hormuz is not a BRICS waterway, it’s Iranian and Omani sovereign waters. BRICS declaration says ‘undisrupted flows’ and ‘protection of critical infrastructure’ but that doesn’t ensure free access to BRICS.

According to information available, the Iranian side met Indian Oil Ministry top brass on BRICS sidelines specifically to offer crude to India.

As a member of both BRICS and the US-led Quad, India must walk a diplomatic tightrope. Pushing too aggressively for de-dollarisation and Rupee-denominated oil trade risks a backlash from Washington, which could jeopardise critical Western technology transfers in strategic sectors like semiconductors and civil nuclear energy.

Ultimately, New Delhi will need to tread cautiously, ensuring its pursuit of strategic autonomy does not come at the cost of its vital partnerships with the West.

Published on September 16, 2026

editorials.title: GST on staffing needs to be reduced
editorials.passage:
India has quietly built one of the world’s three largest formal flexi-staffing industries. A single tax setting is now holding it back from becoming something far larger. The 56th GST Council, meeting on September 3, 2025, delivered the most sweeping tax reform since 2017. GST 2.0 collapsed the old multi-slab regime into two principal rates, 5 per cent and 18 per cent, and moved more than 200 items down, with 99 per cent of goods in the erstwhile 12 per cent slab shifting to 5 per cent from September 22.

The intent: tax essentials lightly, expand consumption, and widen the formal economy. Employment services were left untouched at 18 per cent.

That is the anomaly. For every ₹100 a company now spends on goods taxed at 5 per cent, it pays just ₹5 in tax. Spend the same ₹100 on formal staffing and the levy is ₹18, a 3.6-times gap on labour, the one input no business can do without. Because GST on staffing is charged on the entire invoice, most of which is the worker’s own wage passed through, the burden lands hardest on the sectors we most want to formalise: MSMEs, consumer-facing industries, and GST-exempt services such as healthcare and education that cannot claim input tax credit. The consequences are measurable. Indian Staffing Federation estimates the 18 per cent rate drains ₹20,000-30,000 crore from business liquidity every year and is on course to reduce formal temporary hiring by 10-15 per cent in affected sectors this fiscal, nudging workers back towards informal and gig arrangements that carry no provident fund, no insurance, and no wage protection. Taxing formal employment at a premium, while goods enjoy relief, is a policy working against itself.

Consider what this industry already delivers. Our member companies alone employed 1.83 million formal flexi workers by June 2025, and the organised flexi sector now supports roughly 7.2 million people, about 1.3 per cent of India’s workforce, among the world’s top three flexi-staffing markets. In the last financial year, the sector paid an estimated ₹1.47 lakh crore in wages and ₹52,800 crore towards social security and GST.

Logistics, BFSI and manufacturing together account for around 38 per cent of formal contract employment, with twelve core sectors making up 80 per cent of demand.

Nearly a quarter of these workers are women, and most are young, first-time entrants receiving their very first formal job, complete with EPF, ESI and a bank-credited salary. This is formalisation delivered by the market: jobs, not doles.

The headroom is the real story. India’s flexi penetration, at 1.3 per cent, still trails the US (1.8 per cent) and Europe (1.6 per cent), and it sits against an informal economy that accounts where some 400 million people outside the formal social-security net. Converting even a modest slice of that into organised, contributory employment is, on any reasonable arithmetic, a 20-million-job opportunity. ISF projects the market to compound at over 17 per cent a year towards ₹2.58 lakh crore by FY27, and independent analysis expects the sector to create several million additional livelihoods by 2030. The demand is plainly there; the binding constraint is fiscal, not structural.

Correcting it is not a concession; it is sound revenue policy. Moving employment services to the 5 per cent merit slab would, by our estimate, release up to ₹50,000 crore in cash flows for reinvestment and fresh hiring.

A lower rate applied to a rapidly formalising base does not shrink the tax net; it widens it, through more compliant payroll, more EPF and ESI contributions, and more GST-registered employment.

This is precisely the logic the government itself applied to goods under GST 2.0. Employment deserves the same treatment.

Employment is the most essential input in any economy. Tax it accordingly. Move employment services to 5 per cent, and India can convert a two-million success story into a 20-million one: formalising work, extending social security to millions, and doing it the durable way, through jobs.

The writer is Executive Director, Indian Staffing Federation (ISF)

editorials.title: Trump’s dividend card
editorials.passage:
It is not as if US President Donald Trump took a leaf out of George McGovern’s idea in 1972 that if he won the election that year against Richard Nixon he would give Americans $1000 every year.

But now with about seven weeks to go for the mid-terms, Trump is promising every American adult citizen a dividend cheque of $5,000 if Republicans keep control of the House of Representatives and Senate on November 3.

Some see in this latest offer as a last ditch effort to keep control of Congress. Getting away from the conventional wisdom that the President’s party falls short in the mid-terms, the general thinking — even within the Grand Old Party — is that the numbers would fall short in the House and perhaps even in the Senate. And the White House knows well that should Republicans lose one of the two Chambers this Fall, the US President’s legislative agenda is toast.

Even if Republicans manage to hold on to majorities in Congress, getting funds passed for the latest proposal would be a major problem given that the national debt is already at a whopping $40 trillion.

Americans are not new to dividend cheques, and the latest offer is the third in the series. First was a $5,000 promise in 2025 from all the savings that was going to come from the initiatives of the Department of Governmental Efficiency (DOGE) spearheaded by Elon Musk and Co.

That expected $2 trillions in savings never materialised and few took the numbers put out seriously. And there was this $2,000 dividend cheque floated around, also in the same year, from all the money that was coming America’s way by tariffs.

The US Supreme Court played spoil sport, and now the mad scramble to issue refund cheques to states and companies.

It is said that there are about 245 million citizens who would make up $1.2 trillion in payout for Trump’s idea; and it is not clear if the dividend would cover an estimated five million Americans living overseas.

US Vice-President JD Vance has further qualified telling a media outlet that the money is for the “American middle class” and for “American workers”; and that the amount would be drawn from tariffs collected. All that the White House would say: “President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats’ record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage.”

And there is the legal problem with some taking exception to Trump’s latest proposal on the grounds that it could violate election laws.

Here again a distinction has been made as candidates are allowed to make campaign promises and that cannot be considered illegal vote buying as every adult citizen would be entitled to the money regardless of their individual vote or registration status.

In other words, Trump will have legal protection including a prior Supreme Court ruling to go through with his latest idea. The question is, will voters oblige?

The worry of the White House and of the Republicans seeking re-election in the House and Senate is well founded.

Trump’s approval rating remains stagnant at 33 per cent, his lowest ever and lower than Joe Biden’s rating at this time in 2024. The Iran war is nowhere near a closure with intensified attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz further driving up oil prices.

The only ray of hope for the Grand Old Party is that even if Democrats manage to get the House of Representatives, they will be too far apart internally to put up a united show.

A third Impeachment of Trump is certainly on the cards but chances of getting a conviction in the Senate is between fat, slim and none.

The writer is a senior journalist who has reported from Washington DC on North America and United Nations
