editorials.title: Fuelling Deep-Tech: Building India’s semiconductor product champions via R&D and IP
editorials.passage: By Shivkumar Kalyanraman, CEO, Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), Govt of India India has established formidable depth in semiconductor design and engineering, with its talent contributing to some of the world’s most sophisticated chip programmes. The strategic imperative now is to convert that engineering prowess into enterprise value—building Indian & India-based global semiconductor companies that invest in R&D in India, conceive and commercialise differentiated products, own the intellectual property at their core, and compete at or near the technological frontier in global markets. This is an important distinction. Participation in the semiconductor economy and ownership within it are not the same. India has long supplied high-quality engineering talent to the global technology industry; the greater economic prize lies in converting that intellectual capital into proprietary architectures, products and platforms; and those product decisions are made in India. In an industry where a disproportionate share of value accrues to those who own differentiated technology and IP, the emergence of Indian product companies could fundamentally alter the country’s position in the global semiconductor value chain. ALSO READDefence, semiconductors, rare earths: What PM Modi discussed with Malaysia, Ethiopia, Vietnam Semicon 2.0 can provide an important impetus to this transition. Approved with an outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore, the programme places greater emphasis on chip design, R&D, talent development and the wider semiconductor ecosystem. It builds on the Union Budget 2026–27 announcement of ISM 2.0 with a focus on industry-led research, technology development and skilled workforce creation. The foundations are becoming increasingly substantial. India’s first semiconductor mission, backed by an outlay of ₹76,000 crore, helped catalyse investment in fabrication, packaging and chip design. Under the programme, 12 semiconductor manufacturing projects representing committed investments exceeding ₹1.64 lakh crore have now been approved, with three having commenced commercial production. Semicon 2.0 widens the aperture further—across design, fabrication, advanced packaging, equipment and materials, talent development, and along with ANRF & RDI fund, drives the next phase of R&D in India. For Indian startups, the opportunity is to move up the value chain—from providing semiconductor design and engineering services to building products and creating indigenous IP. Bringing together design support, industry-led R&D, specialised talent and patient venture capital can help promising deep-tech startups make this transition. Capital will be particularly consequential to this transition. Semiconductor ventures operate on timelines and risk profiles fundamentally different from those of conventional software startups, often requiring years of sustained engineering before meaningful revenues begin to materialise. Fabrication, validation and successive design iterations add further layers of cost and complexity, making access to patient, risk-tolerant capital essential. Building enduring semiconductor companies will therefore depend not simply on expanding the pool of available funding, but on cultivating an investment ecosystem with the technical understanding and long-term horizon required to underwrite innovation from early research through commercial scale. ALSO READIndia-US tech ties widen: 6G alliance, semiconductors, AI on the table at G20 Yet capital alone cannot create globally competitive semiconductor companies. It must be complemented by a deeper continuum connecting universities, research institutions, startups and industry, allowing scientific and engineering advances to move more seamlessly from the laboratory into the marketplace. The most consequential semiconductor companies are typically built at this intersection—where specialised research meets entrepreneurial ambition, experienced engineering talent and a clear pathway to commercialisation. Strengthening industry-academia collaboration, expanding access to shared research and prototyping infrastructure, and creating more effective mechanisms for commercialising indigenous research can help turn promising technologies into defensible intellectual property, viable products and, ultimately, globally competitive enterprises. There is already an encouraging base from which to build. More than 100 startups are developing chips under India’s emerging design ecosystem. The challenge ahead is to ensure that the strongest of these ventures can progress from designing a chip to owning a product roadmap, building defensible IP, securing global customers and ultimately scaling into enduring technology enterprises. The ultimate measure of India’s semiconductor ambition will not be how much of the global value chain it can attract, but how much of the future it can create. The real breakthrough will come when chips conceived in India, powered by Indian R&D leading to intellectual property, built into globally competitive products become not the exception, but the signature of India’s technological ascent.

editorials.title: To understand the threat to our real democracy, watch Putin’s fake one
editorials.passage:
M illions of people will participate in elections in Russia this weekend and a new parliament will be chosen, but not necessarily in that order. The purpose of the exercise is to maintain Vladimir Putin’s authority over the political process, which means United Russia, the president’s party, will retain control of the Duma.

That much is settled before the polls open, although the scale of the government’s victory won’t be declared until the votes are counted. A portion of seats is available for other “systemic parties” that function as Kremlin licensed-opposition, padding out the pretence of pluralism. They serve as a pressure valves for public frustration and parliamentary proxies when rival factions within the ruling elite want to nudge Kremlin policy in one direction or another.

The Kremlin likes to minimise the difference between United Russia’s official tally and a number that would plausibly reflect public attitudes to the regime. If the gap is too wide, achieved by fraud too blatant, it conveys insecurity in the Kremlin. Putin’s power doesn’t depend on endorsement by ordinary Russians but his authority is sustained by the illusion that he listens and cares. An egregiously stolen election would prove that he doesn’t.

Everyone knows the result is fixed, but it would breach a social contract if the fiction became too absurd.

Electoral verisimilitude is harder than usual to pull off this time because of war fatigue. No one can pretend any more that the “special military operation” in Ukraine has gone to plan. It was supposed to take weeks and is now in its fifth year. There have been about 1.5 million Russian casualties.

A shortage of volunteers stirs fear that another mobilisation of unwilling army reserves is in the works. Putin has denied that any such draft is required. That he needs to offer public reassurance at all amounts to recognition that progress on the front has stalled and the mood at home has soured.

Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have made the war visible and economically palpable thousands of miles away from the frontline. The veil of state propaganda cannot be drawn across plumes of smoke rising from oil refineries and queues at petrol pumps.

There are no accurate opinion polls in an authoritarian state. Russians are disinclined to share their private thoughts with strangers on the phone, especially when denigrating the armed forces is a criminal offence. A more reliable indicator of growing dissent is the increased rate of its repression. Last month, Yabloko, an inconsequential liberal party, was barred from the elections on a preposterous trumped-up technicality. The real objection was the party’s campaign slogan – “For peace and freedom”.

Yabloko had previously been tolerated as an irrelevant vintage party from the pre-Putin era, not exactly tame but unthreatening; not worth the risk of aggrandisement by political martyrdom. That calculus changed with signs that voters were drifting towards the only available anti-war banner. It wasn’t a big movement but enough to persuade the authorities that denying the party representation after the ballot could be messier than blocking it in advance.

If banning the opposition depresses turnout, all the better. The Kremlin appears to have accepted that a sincere show of enthusiasm for the status quo is unavailable. A boring, low-key election, telling a story of submission and stability, is the next best thing.

Such is the perverse craft of “managed democracy” – the mechanics of running gangster authoritarianism through a notionally liberal constitution. It requires a mix of performative coercion, tactical concession and confected consent. The economic spoils of corruption have to be dispensed widely enough to feed a quiescent elite. There has to be enough theatre of public participation to legitimise the regime. But genuine freedom must also be discredited as the path of chaos.

That has been an easy line to sell to Russians who recall post-Soviet democratisation as a time of rampant gangsterism, surrendered superpower status and national immiseration. Putin is a product of that era and the embodied backlash against it. He transferred the engines of oligarchic capitalist self-enrichment to the reconstituted chassis of a Soviet-style state. He made himself an avatar for imperial nostalgia and an exhausted population’s craving for order. He promised to express the national interest more efficiently as its sole incarnation than any raucous, divided parliament ever could.

That offer has less appeal in established democracies, where political pluralism and the rule of law have deeper roots, but it has an audience. The core proposition – a strong leader to avenge a once great country’s humiliation by foreigners – has twice carried Donald Trump to the White House. His ratings have plummeted but he can still count on credulous adulation from as many as one in three Americans.

What is the equivalent number in Britain? The leading product in this market is Reform UK, which now polls around 23%, level with Labour. Nigel Farage’s position has slipped this year as his personal and party finances have come under scrutiny, but his core supporters are untroubled by the whiff of grubby lucre. For some, convinced that the whole system is a rotten sham, scandal around Reform UK’s receipt of multimillion-pound donations positively burnishes the brand. It proves that Farage is a baller, capable of beating the “establishment” parties at their own game – a gamble that the savvy, loadsamoney crypto crowd are backing.

The deep cynicism feeding that judgment is a vital element in the chemical compound that corrodes democracy. I remember it as the most pungent feature of Russian politics when I lived in Moscow, watching the 90s experiment in democracy fail.

It is the demoralised conviction that no politician would ever be motivated by a spirit of public service. The only categories are weak and strong; suckers and players. To succeed, a nation needs to be led by a strong player. Constitutions and laws are just parts of the toolkit for exercising power. The liberal view that holds them sacred as a system for holding governments to account is the mark of a sucker.

Farage doesn’t put it quite like that. He did tell his party conference last week that an incoming Reform government would declare a “national emergency” to enact a radical agenda within the first 100 days and tolerate no objection from parliament, the courts or Whitehall. No one can say they weren’t warned.

It isn’t an explicitly anti-democratic agenda but it never is with populists in opposition. No one wins elections by promising to cancel future ballots and, as the Russian experience demonstrates, once power has been secured, the well-managed poll is a valuable mechanism for consolidating control.

There is a process of hollowing-out that comes first. It is a relentless corrosion of trust in independent institutions and the sluicing of public debate with caustic cynicism. It is the stirring of disillusionment and frustration into nihilistic rage against the system; sowing division and amplifying despair to make authoritarian rule sound like release from political paralysis.

Russia was lost down that road long ago. British democracy is thankfully more robust, more culturally embedded. Or so we hope. Resilience is not immunity. The Putin model of venal cynicism that dresses authoritarian kleptocracy in a call for national redemption won’t declare its motives in an election campaign. The democratic fightback can’t wait until that election to see how far the poison has spread.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe
editorials.passage:
W henever Donald Trump gives a speech, it’s filled with so many lies and self-serving exaggerations that when he does utter something true, I see that as a sort of marvel. That’s what happened nearly an hour into Trump’s marathon speech last Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention, when he declared: “Only I can make this promise to you.” Trump said that just before he made a promise that was so shameless and irresponsible that what he said was indeed true: only Donald Trump could make such a preposterous promise.

Feeling very generous with other people’s money, Trump promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. It certainly looked and smelled like a bribe.

I guess that when you’re fearing an electoral debacle because your public approval ratings are in the toilet, because people are furious about your disastrous war of choice against Iran and because so many Americans are hopping mad that inflation has risen even though you promised to cut prices, then you might feel the need to take desperate measures, and that’s what Trump did by offering to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s pocket to help sway them to vote Republican.

Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn – that’s more than the Pentagon’s budget and nearly what the US will spend on Medicare this year.

Many Republicans and Trump donors rushed to criticize Trump’s $5,000 plan. Joe Lonsdale, a tech billionaire and Republican donor, said he was “strongly against bread and circus bribes ”, while Representative Bob Good of Virginia, former chair of the House Freedom Caucus, called Trump’s promise a “ socialist vote-buying scheme ”.

What angers me most about Trump’s promise isn’t that it would increase the enormous $40tn federal debt even though Trump once promised to eliminate the entire federal debt . Nor am I angriest about the fact that Trump is essentially seeking to bribe the nation’s entire adult population for short-term political gain while in effect passing the cost on to our children and grandchildren. Trump is unconscionably seeking to finance his bribery by borrowing from future generations.

But here is what makes me angriest: Trump evidently believes that millions and millions of Americans are such rubes that he can bamboozle them into voting Republican because they would want to get their hands on $5,000. I like to think that Americans are smarter than that and won’t be fooled.

When Trump made such a shameless proposal, I couldn’t help but wonder: are there no adults in the room with Trump? Is there no one with a sense of shame or fiscal responsibility who will tell him, “Don’t offer this $5,000 bribe. It stinks to high hell, and it’s grossly irresponsible.”

Some brutal mockery came from Trump’s one-time ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former House member from Georgia. She hasn’t forgotten that Trump promised last fall that thanks to his tariffs, every American, except for high-income people, would receive “ a dividend of at least $2,000” . That didn’t happen. Greene also remembers that when Elon Musk said that Doge would chop the federal budget by $2tn, Trump suggested that a sizable chunk of those savings could go directly to Americans . That didn’t happen either.

Greene taunted Trump by writing on X, “ $5,000 for the peasants will be in the mail after the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.”

Trump egomaniacally called the $5,000 payments a “Trump dividend”, saying the money was available “because of our tremendous strength and success economically ”. But Trump is embellishing big time here; there really hasn’t been economic success during Trump’s second term, other than the much-detested datacenter boom and the stock market hitting repeated records. Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, the trade deficit has jumped over 60% since April, the nation has lost 35,000 factory jobs since Trump’s inauguration, and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations.

After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the money would come from tariff revenues , while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come from charging wealthy foreigners for visas and from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you.

Unfortunately for Trump and every American, Trump’s promise to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s stocking will clash with one of his main promises – the $5,000 payments will increase consumer demand and that will inevitably push up inflation even though Trump repeatedly promised to cut prices .

Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, issued a stern warning about Trump’s $5,000. “Debt is now as large as our entire economy, deficits are running $2tn per year, inflation is about 3.5%, and the 10-year Treasury yield is approaching 5%,” MacGuineas said. “This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation, and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy.”

Kenneth Rogoff, a Harvard economics professor and former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, voiced even more alarm, telling PBS , “The US is already running an unsustainable deficit. This would only blow [it] up even more and increase the already high odds of a debt crisis over next five years.”

With his $5,000 “dividend”, Trump is being his impulsive, myopic and reckless self, just like he was in plunging the US into war against Iran, leaving the nation’s economy and global relations in considerably worse shape than before the war. Trump’s $5,000 promise also risks spooking financial markets and nudging up interest rates.

Every American – Republican, Independent or Democrat – should see through Trump’s shamelessness. If his plan comes to pass, it might be a nice sugar high for many Americans, but it will do real economic damage – to inflation, interest rates and the nation’s debt – and it will also impose an unfair burden on our children and grandchildren.

Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

editorials.title: ‘Pacing’ won’t eliminate the risk of AI doom. Here’s what could
editorials.passage:
W ith Jacob Coxon’s resignation from Anthropic , we have reached the AI risk tipping point. Millions of people are finally coming to understand what experts have known for years: AI companies have been gambling with all of our lives, and the odds are not good.

In response, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has introduced a proposal for “pacing the frontier”, endorsed by Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Can we breathe a sigh of relief? Are we about to step back from the edge of extinction? Amodei envisions a slowdown of one to two years, resulting in “profound progress” on technical safety measures. But that’s not what humanity needs right now. What we need is a plan in which we’re confident AI isn’t going to kill us, and this isn’t it.

The stark reality is this: we don’t know how these AI systems work. We don’t know how to prevent them from misbehaving. We don’t know how to stay in control once they’re smarter than us. We don’t know how to make sure they’re not playing nice or playing dumb to trick our safety tests. We can’t count on solving these problems with another one or two years of research.

I know because I have been researching such problems for more than a decade, including as an AI professor at both the University of Cambridge and the University of Montreal. If we want to reduce the risks from AI to an acceptable level, what we actually need is an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.

Is this really possible? It’s a legitimate question, and geopolitics is the crux: how can countries such as the US and China verify each others’ compliance? Donald Trump recently slammed AI regulation , citing the US’s lead in the AI arms race against Beijing.

But a simple solution is available: de-commission the advanced computer chips necessary to build these AI models. The massive – and already massively unpopular – datacenter build-out could be reversed. The US and China could take turns decommissioning data centers and the chips they contain. If all parties knew that nobody had the means of building more powerful AI, verification would be simple.

To make such an arrangement durable, we could additionally dismantle the supply chain for producing advanced AI chips, which is extremely concentrated and relies on some of the most advanced technology in the world: extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography. Any attempt to operate a covert lithography operation at the scale required for frontier AI development would almost certainly be noticed by other nations’ intelligence services. This plan has benefits over alternative approaches that rely on restricting how computer chips are used. Amodei calls pausing “unlikely”, but an agreement to decommission AI infrastructure would actually be easier to verify than Amodei’s proposals for global coordination, which would require increasing levels of surveillance as computing hardware continues to advance and proliferate.

The economic costs of this plan would be substantial, but given the stakes, unless we have a better plan that actually saves our lives, they are clearly worth it. During the Covid-19 pandemic, governments shut down significant parts of society and the economy to save lives. We should be willing to go to much greater lengths to prevent the extinction of our species. I’m actively researching “softer” versions of the proposal that would involve creating computer chips that can be used to run AI models, but not to build more powerful ones. And other researchers have also developed proposals for an indefinite moratorium.

Amodei’s essay, sadly, does not consider these pause proposals. His plan is ultimately still to have AIs build smarter and smarter AIs with less human involvement – “recursive self-improvement”, a project designed to render humans obsolete.

What should we actually expect to come of Amodei’s plan? Step one would “embed” external evaluators from organizations such as METR , which was invited to investigate the OpenAI-Hugging Face scandal. Big tech CEOs may call this “radical”, but let’s be clear: what they’re actually talking about is more self-regulation.

Three years ago, I helped found the UK AI Security Institute – another leading evaluator. I quit after it was clear the ecosystem was getting the burden of proof formula backwards. Today, AI is still de facto “safe-until-proven dangerous”.

The safety standards Amodei suggests are guaranteed to fall far short of those in other safety-critical industries like aviation. We simply don’t know how to do recursive self-improvement safely.

So let’s stop. Let’s stop making AI we can’t control, and let’s stop listening to the AI industry about how it wants to be regulated. Proposals for a pause are being put forth in both the US and UK legislatures. The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, is coming to Washington to discuss AI, and Trump has an opportunity to make the deal of the century if they can work out how to stop the AI race.

Let’s demand a plan that makes us safe, not just safer.

David Krueger is an assistant professor in Robust, Reasoning and Responsible AI at the University of Montreal. He is also the founder of Evitable , a non-profit that educates the public about the risks of artificial intelligence

editorials.title: It’s my self-care hack of the year: I quit our local veg box scheme, and set my mind free
editorials.passage:
L ast week, as summer gave way to pumpkin season, I found myself contemplating the final squash. Like the horror movie trope of the final girl staggering out of the woods after the massacre, this squash is the sole survivor. All her sister squashes had either been cooked and eaten or left to rot. Now, my killing days were almost over. There would be no sequel.

Or, to put it less dramatically: after six years, we have quit the local organic veg bag collective, which delivered to a nearby pickup point a bag of organic, local seasonal veg once a week. And as a result the mental load and emotional labour of having to contemplate and devise a use for various esoteric kinds of veg is finally, mercifully, over.

I approached the final squash the way I had many, many of her contemporaries. First, I tried to identify her so I could work out how to cook it and whether the skin was edible or not. “Medium-sized frilly orange pumpkin type” I wrote into Google. No match was forthcoming. Then I took a picture of it and did an image search. Still no match. For all its supposed miraculous capabilities, during my own experiments AI has never successfully identified a single pumpkin.

Usually, this is the point where my cortisol soars, but this time it stayed stable: this was the last time that I would expend precious time and energy trying to correctly identify a vegetable, before giving up and doing what I always do, which is chopping it up and roasting it.

Now that it’s done, I cannot tell you how liberated I feel. No more kohlrabi. No more Jerusalem fartichokes. Only my husband will miss the turnips.

Historically, I have always been a great quitter. To use hideous modern parlance, anything that no longer “served” me, whether a job, a relationship, a university course, a country, would always be efficiently dispatched. No looking back.

Leaving the local organic veg collective didn’t feel like this, though. Being a member felt like the right, ethical thing to do (“Don’t be mean about them,” my husband says. “They are a great service”). Raised by a veg box mum – and being a Guardian writer to boot – surely this was my destiny, my birthright? It gave me a warm, self-satisfied glow, albeit an ephemeral one lasting only until I was once again scrubbing layers of caked mud from all of the potatoes just so I could make my kid some sodding chips. “What is this? Wartime?” I muttered to myself.

I’d say my heart hasn’t been in it for at least two years, probably longer, but despite the fact that the relationship had become toxic I felt guilty for wanting to leave. Ever since I had my son, the veg bag has been an albatross. During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip. “More bloody parsnips,” we would sigh, as we unpacked on a Wednesday. “I’m not sure I can do this any more.” Yet another season was always around the corner. The green promise of spring. “Soon! There will be asparagus!” And we would stick it out for another year.

Well, it’s done now, even though I keep picturing Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall shaking his head in disapproval, along with you, dear reader. The veg is more ethical, better for you, and tastier than anything from a supermarket. All of this I acknowledge. Maybe I’m just lazy. And yet, I am a confident – some might say even good – cook. I make meals from scratch, I understand about vitamins and nutritional value. I sometimes open, and look at the pictures in, recipe books by Nigel Slater. It was just that something finally had to give.

It may sound hyperbolic, but getting rid of the veg bag has saved me from a breakdown, possibly. My mental load feels far lighter. “I feel so fucking free, you guys!” I posted, on Instagram, and was inundated with people who had been on the same journey. In some cases, arguing about the rotting veg in the bottom of their fridges was affecting their marriages. We all wanted to do the right thing, it’s just that modern life simply didn’t feel compatible.

I have some fond memories of the veg bag. I’m grateful to the collective for feeding my family. I will miss being a member, especially at Christmas. We joined during the pandemic , when not every item was always available in the shops. My son was weaned on pureed celeriac. We got to try things I never would have otherwise – winter purslane ! Land cress! – and I adored the rainbow chard. The kohlrabi actually made a very nice rosti. Even the final squash was completely and utterly delicious, as if to try to tempt me back. But no. It’s over. And I am finally free.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Big-money donations poison British politics. We can stop the mega-rich buying access and influence
editorials.passage:
T he British people cannot be bought, but their views and votes can be heavily influenced by a flood of political party propaganda – from expensive advertising and constant leaflet drops to personalised online messages targeted directly at voters.

When I fought the election of 2010, there was a massive imbalance in spending. In 2007 we had inherited Labour party debts of £25m following the 2005 election – and with such tight finances Labour was able to spend only £8m in 2010 , in contrast to the Conservatives’ £17m. We lost out in particular by being unable to invest in the new forms of online advertising coming on stream.

But the imbalances are likely to become even starker in future as the recent donations to Reform show. A decade ago, only 1% of individuals and companies making political donations gave of the order of £1m or more. By 2024, they accounted for over a third , at 35%. These latest record-breaking donations from crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne are worth more than all donations to UK political parties in 2025 combined.

Spending more money at an election almost certainly leads to greater electoral success . This is worrying – and while the government recently tasked the Electoral Commission with reviewing campaign spending limits , more must be done. The reforms to election financing recommended by the Commission on the UK’s Future, which I chaired, and in particular a donation cap, should be introduced into the representation of the people bill now in the House of Lords .

Nearly half of voters , with few objecting, say they would view a party more favourably if it introduced a limit on political donations. Indeed, the very fact that money has been openly solicited in return for political access and, potentially, influence – as well as positions of public office and honours – exposes our democracy and weakens public trust.

A cap on individual donations was recommended by the independent Hayden Phillips review in 2007, by the Committee on Standards in Public Life in 2011 – and by an increasing number of senior politicians, including John Major . Indeed, in December 2025, the UK and at least 59 other countries co-sponsored a United Nations resolution that urges state parties to consider “limitations on donations … with a view to combating corruption”.

Other comparable democracies impose donation caps. Canada caps donations to political parties at about £930 annually; France caps donations to political parties at £6,400 annually and £3,900 for presidential campaigns; Italy’s cap is £85,600 per person or company annually.

“My gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k,” Andy Burnham said just before he became prime minister, and in September Stella Creasy and 63 other MPs backed an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which was then withdrawn, to introduce an annual donation cap of £500,000, decreasing to £100,000 after one calendar year.

The new bill should include an enabling power for the secretary of state to set a cap on donations, having consulted the Ethics and Integrity Commission (formerly the Committee on Standards in Public Life) as well as the Electoral Commission.

Some want this cap to include donations by trade unions. But a collection of individual members who provide small contributions and can opt out do not pose the same level of risk to our democracy as multimillion-pound donations from private donors.

Outside general election years, Labour and Conservative party spending has recently been around £60m and £55m , respectively. Transparency International UK has calculated that before 2024, the total spend in election years was about £74m and £87m. In 2024, it says that Labour expenditure ballooned to a record-breaking £103m while the Conservative party spent less – just £74m. But paradoxically, this imbalance was made possible by the Conservative government’s decision to raise general election spending limits .

Donors to the Labour party whom I have met favour a cap on donations; in fact, they say their recent larger-than-normal donations were made simply to even up the odds between political parties.

How would things change? Transparency International UK has made a tool to model the potential impact of donation caps on political party finances. Setting a donation cap of £50,000 per year, you can see the impact of reducing big-money donations. At the same time, there would still be sufficient funding for political parties to campaign effectively and fairly, without a need for additional public funds. It is now time to create such a level playing field.

The reform of political party funding should be the start of a major cleanup of our political system. It is quite wrong that about 100 paid lobbyists sit in an as yet unreformed House of Lords. And it is also wrong that the requirements placed on the lobbying industry to declare its activities are so weak. The British people deserve better.

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

editorials.title: Your photos, your words and your work: why is Labor making it easier for AI companies to take them for free?
editorials.passage:
Leaked documents from a government proposal show that the Albanese government is considering reversing the fundamental rights of Australians under copyright law.

The proposal refers to an “opt-out model”. This would give AI companies permission to train on the open internet here in Australia. Every family photo you ever posted, every small business website, every website would be fair game for AI companies unless you choose to opt out.

Right now, under Australian law, a company has to ask for permission if it wants to use your content. This proposal would mean it doesn’t. It would put the onus on the individual to opt out – through a mechanism that hasn’t yet been proven to work. And it would give AI companies rights to your content until you choose to say no. This flips the legal burden on to the individual. It means that our legal system would serve the interests of AI companies first.

AI companies have scraped on billions of pieces of content globally to train their models. There are more than 200 cases live around the world in which writers, journalists, artists, record labels and publishers are seeking to prove that this training is illegal. Just last year the UK decided to hold firm on copyright law when faced with similar pressure from AI companies – artists including Elton John, Dua Lipa and Paul McCartney led a national campaign to say “no way” – and their government listened.

Artists are at the forefront of this fight as we protect the value that underpins our profession. But this isn’t just about us. This is about protecting the rights of all people to keep their right to decide how their content – their photos, their websites, their written word – is used by AI companies.

Right now, chief executives including Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Elon Musk are begging for global regulation of their technology to prevent the apocalypse. Copyright law is a part of that regulation. It protects individuals and their property. Every other industry, sector, company and individual has to ask for permission before using an individual’s work – trillion-dollar AI companies must do the same.

If the most powerful companies in the world can’t properly licence the content they are training on, or if they can’t create the technology to license their training content properly, we must seriously question their technical and civil competency. They can solve diseases, fight wars, they might kill us all, but they can’t licence the content that makes their model “intelligent” in the first place? Seriously.

Talk about self-control, regulation and “needing governments to step in” – well, copyright law is a start. Everyone else in our society abides by copyright law – we don’t steal other peoples stuff. We ask them permission to use it.

If the Albanese government and the Coalition are requesting that the Australian people weaken their own rights for the benefit of the world’s biggest technology companies, they must explain the benefit transparently to Australians.

Giving AI companies access to every piece of content that Australians have shared online without their permission or consent is a matter of grave concern for national security itself.

The Albanese government must put this to the Australian people – do Australians want to let AI companies train on every piece of content they have ever put online, without permission and consent? Or do Australians want the government to be a global leader and force AI companies to train their models legally and with the consent of the people?

Holly Rankin is an artist professionally known as Jack River and the executive director of Sentiment Group, a government affairs and strategic communications firm

editorials.title: Why is the White House being so weird about Natalie Harp again?
editorials.passage:
P assport, money, emotional support human: Donald Trump had all the travel essentials on his recent trip to Ireland . The president flew into Dublin on Saturday morning to play golf, meet the country’s leaders and make provocative comments about unification . Melania didn’t accompany her husband on the trip (“Uh, she sends her regards,” Trump said), but his devoted aide Natalie Harp was obviously at his side.

You’ll know Harp: the 35-year-old assistant was headline news last month after Democratic senator Jon Ossoff quipped that Trump didn’t want to do his job; he just wanted to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”. That comment would have been quickly forgotten were it not for the Trump administration’s unhinged response (sample: “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics”), which sparked a media frenzy. There was suddenly a spotlight on Harp, who is nicknamed the “human printer” because she trails the president with a portable printer, ready to hand him hard copies of flattering coverage. She appears to be disturbingly obsessed with her boss and he seems to appreciate the attention: it was recently revealed that Trump gave her (and two other female aides) a cash gift of $45,000 (£33,000) for a nice holiday.

Harp may be a subject of intrigue, but the news cycle is frenetic. The human printer’s recent business trip to Ireland would not have been particularly noteworthy were it not for the fact that the White House is once again being extremely weird about it. On Saturday, the independent journalist Aaron Rupar posted a photo of the aide with the comment: “Look who made the trip to Ireland! #TravelWithNatalie.” This appeared to incense the White House’s Rapid Response 47 X account, which issued a personal attack in reply. “President Trump does, in fact, travel with staff,” they wrote . “Aaron, on the other hand, is a sick, deluded freak (in his 40s) who sits behind a keyboard and posts creepy things like this.”

Sick deluded freaks in glass houses probably shouldn’t throw stones. And while we’re on the subject of best practices: anyone working in a professional comms capacity should probably understand that ignoring Rupar’s tweet would have been the sensible thing to do. Instead, they chose to amplify it and get people talking about the Harp-Trump relationship again.

Which leads us to a question that comes up frequently in the Trump era: is all this some sort of cunning distraction technique? Does Team Trump prefer it if people are focused on Harp rather than Iran or the Epstein files or the economy? Or, alternatively, does the president just surround himself with idiots? My money is on the latter.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: China does not need to replace the US in the Gulf
editorials.passage:
China’s diplomatic calendar this year reflects its growing international weight. A succession of prominent leaders has travelled to Beijing, including those from the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, Canada, Spain, South Korea, Pakistan and Jordan.

The recent visit by Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani to China, as well as visits by high-level officials from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia earlier this year, confirm Beijing’s expanding role in the Gulf.

The region, which has traditionally aligned with the US, is seeing growing competition between the two powers. But this rivalry does not mean that China is seeking to replace the US. It is approaching the region through trade and technology – something that fits into the Gulf’s own economic and development interests.

The US remains the Gulf’s most important external military partner. Its defence partnerships, intelligence ties, weapons systems, naval capabilities, and military presence remain central to regional security.

For years, Washington has measured Chinese influence against its own military power. By those standards, China remains far from being able to replace the US. But that is the wrong measure of strategic success.

China has shown little interest in competing with the US on military reach in the Gulf. That is because it has benefitted directly from the security Washington has provided in the region.

For decades, the US Navy helped secure maritime routes through which Gulf energy reached Asian markets. US military power in the Gulf region contributed to the stability that allowed Chinese companies to trade, invest, build infrastructure, and purchase energy.

From the Chinese perspective, this arrangement cost little and delivered significant returns. Replacing the US security system would mean assuming the political, financial and military costs of becoming the Gulf’s security guarantor, which would not be in its interest.

Instead, China has concentrated on sectors where it can build economic leverage, seeking to become as important to Gulf states’ economies as Washington is in the region’s security architecture.

Today, Chinese state-owned firms hold stakes in key Gulf infrastructure, such as ports. For example, COSCO Shipping Ports holds a controlling stake in the joint venture operating the CSP Abu Dhabi Terminal at Khalifa Port in the UAE.

Chinese companies are also increasingly connected to sectors that will shape the region’s future, including renewable energy, telecommunications, manufacturing, logistics, electric vehicles, and digital infrastructure.

Once these systems become interconnected through financing, contracts, and trade, disengagement carries substantial economic costs. An aircraft carrier can leave, and a troop deployment can be reduced, but leverage and stakes in ports, factories, telecommunications networks, and supply chains are harder to undo.

China’s approach does not require Gulf governments to become politically pro-Beijing. It only needs an openly anti-China position to become economically too costly.

For the Gulf states, there is no contradiction in seeking strong ties with both powers. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar each want US security cooperation and advanced Western technology while also seeking Chinese markets, manufacturing capacity, investment, and access to Asian economic networks.

Their objective is to avoid excessive dependence on either power. Their strategy is pursuing diversification, hedging, and strategic autonomy in an increasingly multipolar international system.

The US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged US bases across the Gulf, including Al Udeid in Qatar, demonstrated why this strategy is so crucial. Excessive dependence on a single actor or area creates vulnerability, whether that dependence involves a single security provider, export market, shipping route, technology ecosystem, or source of capital.

For the Gulf states, diversification is therefore a necessity, a form of risk management. They are positioning themselves for an international system in which US power remains important but is no longer the only source of economic, political, and technological influence.

Diversification is being pursued not just in the security sphere. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and other regional states are attempting to build economies beyond hydrocarbons. Artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, renewable energy, and logistics are becoming central to their national strategies.

Artificial intelligence (AI) in particular shows what is at stake. Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN and the UAE’s G42 reflect national ambitions to build AI industries. AI in turn depends on advanced chips, data centres, energy, computing infrastructure, capital, and skilled workers.

The Gulf states are seeking partners who can contribute to the capital, technology, infrastructure, and industrial partnerships required to build these more diversified economies.

Washington should therefore reconsider how it measures strategic power.

The decisive question may no longer be how many bases a country possesses in a region, but how difficult that country is to remove from the regional system.

The US remains deeply embedded in the Gulf through defence relationships, intelligence cooperation, financial institutions, universities, technology companies, and diplomatic partnerships.

China is creating a different form of integration, as trade, infrastructure, technology, and investment generate long-term interests that markets can translate into leverage.

Washington need not force Gulf governments to choose between the US and China in every sector. Legitimate security concerns remain over advanced semiconductors, artificial intelligence, telecommunications, sensitive data, and dual-use technologies. Those sectors require clear safeguards.

The US’s better option is to compete. It should offer superior technology, credible financing, and deeper industrial partnerships, playing a meaningful role in the Gulf’s economic transformation.

Security guarantees remain essential, but they no longer guarantee primacy across every sector.
